windows.fallback: falls back to a native ProfileList registry enumeration (no login count) when the Security channel is inaccessible
requires an elevated token to read the Security channel; reports an error otherwise

caveats: **`session_history` columns on Linux and macOS do not match the declared schema.** The Windows leg fills `event_type|logon_type|source|timestamp|detail` as named, but the Linux and macOS leg splits `last`'s first three tokens and writes the tty, the host token, a derived `console`/`remote`/`system` class, a `completed`/`active`/`crash` word and the rest of the line into those same slots. The real date and duration exist only as free text in `detail`, so do not consume those two OSes' output as if it matched the Windows or YAML meaning. The window is the latest `count` records (1 to 500, default 50 on an out-of-range value) and includes `reboot` lines.

**`primary_user` is a recent-activity heuristic, not a usage measurement.** It counts account names in the latest 200 Windows 4624 events (every logon type, so network and service logons count, and machine accounts and `SYSTEM` are dropped) or the latest 200 lines of `last` (boilerplate lines dropped); a tie goes to the alphabetically first name. When the Windows Security log cannot be read it falls back to the last profile under `\Users\` in registry order with `login_count` `0`, and sets no status.

**The admin and group answers are narrow.** Windows `local_admins` looks up the group literally named `Administrators` and, if that lookup fails (for example on a localised Windows), writes no rows, no error row and no status, which reads like a host with no administrators. `group_members` accepts only the characters `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -` and no leading `-` or `.`, so a group with a space in its name, such as `Remote Desktop Users`, is rejected with an `Invalid group name` row on every OS. Linux `group_members` finds primary-group members by scanning `/etc/passwd` only.

**`local_users` is a best-effort account list.** Linux and macOS leave out system accounts (uid below 1000 and 500, and `_` names on macOS), and on Linux `last_logon` is the raw `lastlog` line, `unknown` for a name outside the safe character set, and `Never` when `lastlog` says so. `enabled` on Linux and macOS means a usable login shell, not an unlocked password, and the Windows `last_logon` is this machine's own record shown in the agent's local time.

**A minimal or locked-down host can look empty.** An image without `last` or `lastlog` degrades `local_users`, `primary_user` and `session_history` to `UNAVAILABLE`, while `logged_on` (`utmp`), `local_admins` and `group_members` (`getgrnam`) are unaffected. Because a tool's exit code is ignored, an unreadable `wtmp` gives the same `last command failed` row as a missing tool but with no status, and `group_members` returning zero rows with no `error` row means the group exists with no members.

definitions.description: Lists members of a specified local group. On Windows queries NetLocalGroupGetMembers and reports member type (user, group, well_known_group, alias). On Linux reads /etc/group and checks primary GID assignments in /etc/passwd. On macOS reads the group via dscl. The group name is a required parameter.

Lists members of the local Administrators group. On Windows this queries the Administrators group via NetLocalGroupGetMembers and reports member type (user, group, well_known_group, alias) and domain. On Linux checks sudo/wheel groups plus root. On macOS reads the admin group via dscl.

Enumerates local user accounts on the endpoint. Reports the username, enabled/disabled status, last logon timestamp, and account description. On Linux reads /etc/passwd (skipping system accounts with UID < 1000), on macOS uses dscl, on Windows uses NetUserEnum. On macOS, also reports console_state — a tri-state ("true"/"false"/"unknown") signal for whether the account is the current GUI/console-login user; Linux and Windows omit this field entirely rather than leaving it empty. On Linux, a username containing characters outside [A-Za-z0-9._-] skips the lastlog lookup and reports last_logon as "unknown".

Enumerates currently logged-on users on the endpoint. Reports each user's name, domain/host, logon type (console, RDP, remote), and session identifier. Uses WTS APIs on Windows, utmp on Linux, and the 'who' command on macOS.

Identifies the primary user of the endpoint by analyzing login frequency. On Windows queries Security Event Log for Event ID 4624 (logon) events and counts occurrences per user, falling back to the registry profile list when the Security channel is unreadable. On Linux and macOS parses the output of the 'last' command instead, capped at the 200 most recent lines. Returns the user with the most login events and the count. On Windows, machine accounts (ending with $) and SYSTEM are excluded from the Security Event Log count; on Linux/macOS, 'last' boilerplate lines (reboot, shutdown, wtmp) are excluded instead.

Shows historical login and logout session records. On Windows queries the Security Event Log for Event IDs 4624 (logon) and 4634 (logoff), parsing logon type, source address, and timestamps. On Linux and macOS parses the 'last' command output instead — the six output fields are populated positionally from 'last', not from the same event-log semantics as Windows: the "event_type" field carries the tty, "logon_type" carries last's host/source token, "source" carries the derived console/remote/system classification, "timestamp" carries the completed/active/crash status, and the real date/time lives in "detail" as free text. The count parameter controls how many records to return (clamped to 1-500). Requires elevated privileges on Windows to read the Security event log.

Lists active interactive sessions on the endpoint, including session state (Active, Connected, Disconnected, Idle), the connected user, remote client name or host, and idle time. Uses WTS session APIs on Windows and the 'w' command on Linux/macOS. The idle field is always "0" on Windows — idle-time decoding is not implemented there.

description: Reports logged-on users, sessions, local accounts, admin group members, group membership, primary user, and session history
how_it_works:
All seven actions are reads: nothing in this plugin creates, changes or deletes an account, session or group. `logged_on` and `sessions` answer "who is on this host right now" from the OS session table (Windows Terminal Services sessions, Linux `utmp`, macOS `who` and `w`). `local_users`, `local_admins` and `group_members` list accounts and group membership from the OS's own directory (the Windows NetAPI, `/etc/passwd` and `getgrnam` on Linux, `dscl` on macOS); `group_members` takes a group name, `local_admins` is a fixed lookup of the admin group. `primary_user` and `session_history` mine recent login history: the Security event log on Windows, `last` on Linux and macOS. `primary_user` reduces that window to the one account with the most login records; `session_history` returns the records themselves, newest first, up to `count`. On Linux and macOS every external tool (`w`, `last`, `lastlog`, `who`, `dscl`) runs through a bounded argv runner with no shell and a 10 second deadline, and a tool that cannot be started, times out or is killed is reported through the result status instead of reading as an empty list. Windows runs no subprocess. The plugin is deliberately not an authorisation view: it reports what the OS records, not who is entitled to what.

### What you can decide with it

| Question | Action | Windows | macOS | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Who is signed in now, and from where? | `logged_on` | Active and disconnected sessions that have a user name; `RDP` when the session name says so | `who` lines; remote when the tty is `ttys*` | `utmp` user-process entries only, so a session that does not register in `utmp` is not seen; remote when the tty is `pts/*` |
| What state is each session in, and how long idle? | `sessions` | Every session with a user name, with its real state (Active, Connected, Disconnected, Idle, Listen); idle is always `0` | `w -h` lines, state always `Active`, idle as `w` prints it | Same as macOS |
| Which local accounts exist, are they enabled, when did they last log on? | `local_users` | Local accounts from `NetUserEnum`, enabled flag from the account-disabled bit | `dscl` accounts with uid 500 or above, plus `root`, not starting `_`; enabled means the shell is not `false` or `nologin` | `/etc/passwd` accounts with uid 1000 or above, plus `root`; enabled means the shell is not `nologin` or `false`. Directory-service accounts are not listed |
| Who holds administrator rights locally? | `local_admins` | Direct members of the group named `Administrators`; a nested group appears as one `group` row and is not expanded | Direct members of the `admin` group | Members listed on the `sudo` and `wheel` groups, plus the uid 0 account |
| Who is in a given group? | `group_members` | Direct members of the named local group | Members from `dscl` | Listed members, plus accounts in `/etc/passwd` whose primary group it is (`primary_group`) |
| Who normally uses this device? | `primary_user` | Most frequent account in the latest 200 logon events | Most frequent account in the latest 200 lines of `last` | Same as macOS |
| Who logged in or out recently? | `session_history` | Logon and logoff events (4624 and 4634) with logon type, source address and UTC time | Lines of `last`, newest first | Same as macOS |

What a clean result does and does not prove. An empty `logged_on` or `sessions` is a legitimate answer (nobody is signed in) and carries no status; only the typed result status tells a degraded read from a clean empty one. A `local_admins` or `group_members` list is the direct, local view only: it does not follow nested groups, directory-service groups or `sudoers` rules, so it is not the set of people who can become administrator. `primary_user` and `session_history` see only the latest window of the login records, so they say nothing about a long-quiet account, and a host with the Security log cleared, or without logon auditing, returns nothing useful on Windows. Nothing here proves an account is in use: `enabled` reflects the account-disabled flag on Windows and the login shell on Linux and macOS, not a password lock or expiry.

### Diagrams

#### Which action answers which question

The first two read the live session table, the next three read the account directory, and the last two read recorded history. Only `group_members` and `session_history` take a parameter.

#### How a Security-log read can fail on Windows

`session_history` fails loudly: the status and the error row both name the cause. `primary_user` prefers an answer, so when the Security log cannot be read it names a profile from the registry instead, and that answer carries no status; tell it apart by `source` `profile_list` and a login count of `0`. The fallback picks the last profile under `\Users\` in registry order, which says nothing about who actually uses the host.

outputs_note: Rows are pipe-delimited, one per record, and start with a literal discriminator (`user`, `session`, `local_user`, `admin`, `group_member`, `primary_user` or `session_history`). `logged_on`, `sessions` and `group_members` write zero rows, not a placeholder, when there is nothing to report; only the typed result status separates a degraded read from a clean empty one. A query-level problem (missing or invalid parameter, group not found, tool not found) writes a single `<discriminator>|error|<message>` row (for example `group_member|error|Group not found: x` or `admin|error|query failed`; on Linux an unreadable `/etc/passwd` writes `local_user|error|false|Never|<message>`). `local_users` varies its field count by OS: Windows and Linux rows carry four data fields, macOS rows carry five (`console_state` is appended). On Linux, `last_logon` is the account's `lastlog` line verbatim, not the formatted timestamp the table below describes (caveat 4). On Linux and macOS `session_history` writes `last`'s columns into the declared fields in a different order (caveat 1), and `sessions` always reports state `Active` on those two systems.

privileges.grant: None for the five actions that use WTS and NetAPI calls. `session_history`, and the first path of `primary_user`, read the Security event log, which needs Security-log read access: LocalSystem has it. For the intended virtual account the privilege model lists `Event Log Readers` membership, and says the Security log additionally needs `SeSecurityPrivilege` (`docs/agent-privilege-model.md`; not measured under that account)
privileges.if_refused: `session_history` reports `PERMISSION_DENIED` with `users_win_events:access_denied` and an `error` row; `primary_user` falls back to the ProfileList registry (see the diagram above)
privileges.measured: Sample captured as `SYSTEM` on bare metal

privileges.grant: None: every leg is a plain `dscl`, `who`, `w` or `last` call or the shared console-user read, with no privileged open
privileges.if_refused: A tool that cannot start, times out or is signalled is forwarded as `UNAVAILABLE` or `CONSTRAINED`; the action then writes its own `unknown` or `error` row text
privileges.measured: Sample captured as a normal interactive user (euid 501), not as the root daemon; all seven actions returned rows

privileges.grant: None for the native legs (`utmp`, `getgrnam`, `getpwuid`, `/etc/passwd`). `w`, `last` and `lastlog` must be installed; they read the login records the OS keeps (`utmp`, `wtmp`, `lastlog`)
privileges.if_refused: A missing or failed tool is forwarded as `UNAVAILABLE` or `CONSTRAINED`; `logged_on`, `local_admins` and `group_members` do not depend on a tool and are unaffected
privileges.measured: Sample captured as `euid 0` in a minimal container with neither `last` nor `lastlog`; not measured as `yuzu-agent`
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, dedicated unprivileged account (`yuzu-agent` on the packaged unit), never root by design; the privilege model has no row for this plugin

result_status.when: default; every OS tool or native call finished normally. This is the status of every clean or intentionally empty read, such as an empty `logged_on`
`primary_user` stopped `last` at its 200-line bound while it was still producing output. This is deliberate truncation, not a failure, and is the normal case on any host with a longer history
a POSIX tool ran past the 10 second deadline, was cancelled, or was killed by a signal
no binary was found at the probed paths, or the spawn failed (the Linux container sample, which has no `last` or `lastlog`)
Windows Security channel query denied; for `primary_user` only when the ProfileList fallback also failed
Windows Security channel missing or unavailable
the Windows event read made no progress for 10 seconds
any other Windows event query or read error

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result only.** Rows travel the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response and land in the `ResponseStore` (default 90-day retention), readable at `/api/responses/{id}`.

**Not consumed by** daily-sync inventory, the TAR warehouse, DEX or metrics. Nothing in this plugin runs on a schedule; each definition's `gather.ttlSeconds` (60 to 300 seconds) is a repeat-query cache lifetime, not a cron trigger.

**Sensitivity.** Every action's rows name specific accounts: `username` and `member_name` (local and logged-on accounts, including administrators), `domain` or `domain_or_group` (a Windows domain or host name), and Windows `session_history` carries the source IP address of each logon. On Linux and macOS `session_history` and `sessions` can carry the remote host or client name a user connected from, and `local_users` carries the account's display name or comment. No column carries installed-software data.

**Siblings.** The `core.crossplatform.users` instruction set (`content/definitions/users_set.yaml`, "User Account Management") bundles the `logged_on`, `sessions`, `local_users` and `local_admins` definitions of this same plugin; this plugin has no action that creates, disables or reassigns an account.

**MCP / REST.** Discover with `discover_plugins` (summary) then `yuzu://plugin-docs` (this page as data) and `get_definition("device.users.session_history")`; run with `execute_instruction {definition_id, parameters}`; read results at `/api/responses/{id}`.
